listeningScripts.title: Booking a Self-Storage Unit
listeningScripts.text:
Clerk: Good afternoon, Fairfield Self Storage, Daniel speaking.
Caller: Hello. I need to store some furniture while I move house, and I wanted to ask about your units.
Clerk: Certainly. Can I take your name first?
Caller: It's Helena Braithwaite. That's B-R-A-I-T-H-W-A-I-T-E.
Clerk: Thank you. And a mobile number?
Caller: 07946 512 380.
Clerk: Lovely. Now, roughly how much are you storing?
Caller: The contents of a two-bedroom flat, so a sofa, a bed, a dining table and about twenty boxes.
Clerk: In that case I'd recommend the medium unit. It's seventy-five square feet, which takes a two-bedroom load comfortably.
Caller: And what does that cost?
Clerk: The medium unit is thirty-eight pounds per week. There's no deposit, but there is a one-off admin charge of twenty pounds when you open the account.
Caller: Fine. When could I start?
Clerk: We have units free from the ninth of April. Would that suit?
Caller: The ninth is perfect. How long can I keep it?
Clerk: There's no maximum. The minimum booking is four weeks, and after that you can leave whenever you like with one week's notice.
Caller: Good. Is there anything I'm not allowed to store?
Clerk: The main restriction is anything flammable — paint, fuel, gas cylinders. Food is also prohibited because it attracts pests.
Caller: That's all fine. How do I get in?
Clerk: You'll be issued with an access code rather than a key, so there's nothing to lose. The site is open from six in the morning until ten at night, seven days a week.
Caller: And is it insured?
Clerk: Your goods aren't covered automatically — you'd need to add our cover, which is four pounds a week for up to five thousand pounds of contents. Most customers take it.
Caller: I'll take that as well, please. Do I need to bring anything on the day?
Clerk: Just photographic identification — a passport or driving licence — and we'll do the paperwork at reception. Oh, and it's worth knowing that we sell packing materials on site, so if you run short of boxes you don't need to go anywhere.
Caller: That's very helpful. So that's the medium unit, from the ninth of April, with insurance.
Clerk: That's right. I'll send confirmation by email — could I take the address?
Caller: It's h.braithwaite@mailbox.com.
Clerk: Perfect. You'll have that within the hour.

listeningScripts.title: Volunteer Induction at a Botanic Garden
listeningScripts.text:
Coordinator: Right, could everyone gather round? Thank you all for volunteering at Ashcroft Botanic Garden — I'm Priya, and I coordinate the volunteer programme.

Let me start with some practical points. Volunteer sessions run every Tuesday and Saturday, and we ask for a minimum commitment of one session a fortnight rather than every week, because we've found that people who promise more than they can manage tend to stop coming altogether. The garden opens to the public at ten, so volunteers arrive at nine — that hour before opening is when most of the work gets done.

Now, the thing new volunteers most often ask about is what they'll actually be doing. It is not, I'm afraid, mostly planting. The great majority of the work is weeding, watering, sweeping paths and clearing dead material, and the planting that visitors imagine is a small fraction of the year's activity. I say this plainly because it's the mismatch between expectation and reality that loses us most people in the first month.

We do offer training. Everyone does a half-day induction covering safety and tool use, and after three months you can apply for the propagation course, which is the one most people are after. Places on it are limited to eight per year, so it's allocated by how long you've been with us rather than first come first served.

Let me tell you about the site itself. As you come through the main entrance, the visitor centre is immediately on your right — that's where you sign in and collect tools. Directly opposite it, on the left of the entrance path, is the tropical glasshouse, which is the tall building with the curved roof. If you follow the main path north past the glasshouse, the walled garden is at the far end on the left-hand side. The pond sits in the middle of the site, and the alpine rockery is on the east side of the pond, facing it. Finally, the tool store — which is where you'll be heading on most mornings — is behind the visitor centre, tucked into the south-east corner of the site.

One last point. Please don't talk to visitors about plant identification unless you're confident, and please do wear the green tabard at all times, because visitors will ask you questions whether or not you know the answers, and the tabard is how they tell you apart from other visitors.

listeningScripts.title: Discussing a Travel Survey
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: So, Ravi and Cerys, you're presenting your travel survey next week. How's it going?
Ravi: Reasonably well. We surveyed two hundred and forty students about how they get to campus.
Cerys: Though we had to change the method halfway through.
Tutor: Why was that?
Cerys: We started with an online form, and after two weeks we'd only had thirty responses. So we switched to stopping people at the campus entrances with tablets.
Ravi: Which worked much better — we got the remaining two hundred and ten in four days.
Tutor: That's a substantial improvement. Any drawback?
Ravi: One, and it took us a while to see it. Standing at the entrances means we only surveyed people who came to campus, so anyone studying entirely from home is invisible in our data.
Tutor: Good — that's exactly the kind of limitation the examiners want to see identified. What did you find?
Cerys: The headline is that forty-two per cent walk, which was much higher than we expected.
Ravi: I'd predicted the bus would dominate. It's second, at twenty-eight per cent.
Cerys: Cycling was only nine per cent, which surprised us both given the new cycle lanes.
Tutor: Did you ask why?
Cerys: We did, and the answer wasn't the weather, which is what we assumed. It was storage — people said they had nowhere secure to leave a bike at the halls of residence.
Tutor: That's a useful finding because it points at something the university can actually change. Now, what about your presentation itself?
Ravi: We've got twenty minutes. I'm doing the method and Cerys is doing the findings.
Tutor: Can I suggest reversing that? Start with the finding that surprised you, then explain how you got there. Audiences give you their attention for the first two minutes and you're currently spending those on sampling procedure.
Ravi: That's fair.
Tutor: And keep your slides to the numbers you'll actually discuss. The commonest fault in these presentations is a table of everything, from which the speaker reads three figures.
Cerys: What about the limitations — should those go at the end?
Tutor: Put them where they arise, next to the finding they qualify. At the end they sound like an apology; beside the result they sound like judgement.

listeningScripts.title: Birds in Cities
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: Today I want to look at why some birds thrive in cities while their close relatives disappear from them, because the answer turns out to be less about tolerance of people than you might assume.

The first thing to say is that the urban environment is not simply a degraded version of the countryside. It is warmer — city centres run several degrees above the surrounding land — it is lit at night, it is noisier, and its food supply is abundant, unpredictable in location and highly reliable in total. Any species that can exploit that combination does extremely well, and the species that cannot are not merely reduced but absent.

The trait that predicts urban success most strongly is not body size or diet breadth, as was long assumed, but behavioural flexibility — the willingness to try an unfamiliar food source or nest site. Species that will nest on a ledge as readily as in a tree, and will investigate an unfamiliar object rather than avoid it, colonise cities repeatedly and independently. Those that require a specific nesting substrate do not, however common they are outside.

Noise is the constraint that has produced the most interesting adaptation. Urban traffic noise is concentrated at low frequencies, and birdsong at those frequencies is masked, so several species in cities sing at a higher pitch than the same species in nearby woodland. There is an active argument about whether this is learned adjustment within a lifetime or genuine change across generations, and the evidence at present favours the first.

Artificial light has effects that are easier to measure and harder to interpret. Birds in lit areas begin singing earlier, sometimes hours before dawn, and breed earlier in the year. Whether that earlier breeding helps or harms depends entirely on whether the food they need has also shifted earlier, and in many cases it has not, which produces a mismatch between the hungriest period for the chicks and the peak abundance of insects.

I want to finish with the point that matters for anyone designing a city. What supports urban bird populations is not the total area of green space but its connectedness and its structural complexity — a series of small gardens with shrubs, dead wood and varied planting supports more species than a single large mown lawn of the same total area. That finding is consistent across studies and is almost always ignored, because a lawn is cheaper to maintain and easier to photograph.
